case_study_insert.main_stem: Kite Digital Studio (KDS) is a private limited company in the mobile app development and digital services sector, employing a workforce of 35. Founded in 2015 by Daniel Okafor, who still takes all major decisions, the business operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. KDS plans to invest $640,000 in an automated app-testing suite with e-commerce payment integration, financed by a $400,000 seven-year bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $280,000 a year, a variable cost of $12 a unit and a selling price of $40, and currently produces 25,000 units a year. KDS faces a quality problem: the defect rate in released apps has risen to 3.6% and client complaints about late delivery are growing.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Report — Q3 2025: KDS released 1,400 app builds, with a defect rate of 3.6%, up from 1.9% a year ago. A quality control inspection of the latest release confirmed the faults, and client complaints rose from 26 to 47 per month, while average delivery time is 6.5 days. A survey of 250 small-business clients found 68% want faster updates and 44% would pay $2 more per month for priority support. Off-the-job quality assurance courses at the local college cost $950 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Kite Digital Studio for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.5% to 4.2%. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.1% from $14.80 to $15.70 per hour from January 2027. (3) Cloud-server and software licence input costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year, and digital-services spending grew 5.5% in the same period.

questions.question_text: KDS is financing part of its app-testing expansion with a seven-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for KDS of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit requires no interest payments or fixed repayments, so KDS keeps cash that would otherwise service the $400,000 seven-year bank loan. That cash can fund quality assurance training at $950 per employee and the integration work on the $640,000 app-testing suite, helping reduce the 3.6% defect rate without increasing the $280,000 annual fixed costs.

Point 2: Internal funding leaves Daniel Okafor's autocratic control unchallenged, since no lender can impose covenants on how the 35-strong studio operates. Using $240,000 retained profit also avoids putting the business's assets at risk if the 47 monthly complaints and 6.5-day delivery time are not improved quickly, which protects the firm while it tries to win back small-business clients. The 44% who would pay $2 more for priority support indicate that cash generated internally can be reinvested in service improvements, whereas interest on the $400,000 loan would leave less to spend on the 35 developers tackling quality.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to KDS and its financing decision.

questions.question_text: KDS is launching its new automated app-testing suite. Consider trade-journal advertising, industry conference sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should KDS choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade-journal advertising: Advertisements in software trade journals reach an audience of professional developers and could build credibility for the $640,000 app-testing suite. The cost is moderate, but readership is declining and the message is static, so it may not reach the 250 small-business clients who want faster updates and who compare tools online.

Industry conference sponsorship: Sponsoring a developers' conference puts KDS in front of decision-makers and allows live demonstrations, which suits a technical product. However, stand and travel costs are high for a 35-employee firm servicing a $400,000 loan, and only a limited number of delegates attend, so the reach is narrow compared with the 1,400 app builds a year the suite must support.

Social media influencer marketing: Technology reviewers can demonstrate the testing suite to a large online audience at relatively low cost, with measurable clicks. This suits the 68% of surveyed clients who want faster updates and the 44% who would pay $2 more for priority support, and it can address the 3.6% defect rate story honestly by showing how the new suite catches faults before release.

Recommendation: KDS should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the online buyer cheaply and can demonstrate product quality, unlike static journals, and it scales beyond a single conference. Trade-journal advertising is rejected as low-reach and outdated; conference sponsorship is rejected as expensive and too narrow for a firm needing 25,000 units of volume. With complaints already at 47 per month and delivery at 6.5 days, KDS needs a promotion that can highlight improvements quickly; an influencer demonstration can be updated, unlike a printed journal advert or a fixed conference stand.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to KDS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two options in the context of KDS with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options with a well-justified recommendation explaining why journals and conferences are rejected.

questions.question_text: KDS has a rising defect rate and growing complaints about late delivery. Explain two benefits for KDS of using autocratic leadership within its hierarchical structure to improve quality.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Daniel Okafor set one clear quality standard for all 1,400 app builds, which is useful when the defect rate has risen from 1.9% to 3.6%. With authority concentrated at the top, a decision to hold a defective release can be enforced immediately, protecting the 250 small-business clients from further faults and reducing the 47 complaints per month.

Point 2: The hierarchical structure gives each of the 35 staff a defined place in the chain of command, so responsibility for the 6.5-day delivery time is unambiguous and errors can be traced quickly. Clear instructions and close supervision suit a studio trying to integrate the $640,000 automated testing suite, because developers know exactly which testing steps are required and cannot bypass them unnoticed. Clear top-down standards are especially useful when 1,400 builds a year must be checked, because the 35 developers know exactly who is responsible for the rise to 3.6% defects and for the 47 complaints.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to KDS's defect rate, complaints and delivery time.

questions.question_text: KDS wants to reduce the defect rate in released apps. Consider quality control inspection or quality assurance prevention. Which should KDS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Quality control inspection: Inspecting finished app builds before release can catch the faults behind the 3.6% defect rate and stop defective software reaching the 250 clients. It is straightforward to introduce and gives immediate results, but it is reactive: errors are already built in, so rework adds to the 6.5-day delivery time and may worsen the 47 monthly complaints about late delivery.

Quality assurance prevention: Building quality into each development stage prevents faults rather than finding them later, which suits an automated testing suite worth $640,000. The insert states off-the-job quality assurance courses cost $950 per employee, but it does not say how many of the 35 staff need training, so no defensible total can be invented. Prevention reduces rework and protects the $40 selling price, though benefits appear only after staff change their routines.

Decision: KDS should choose quality assurance prevention, supported by a final inspection as a backstop. It attacks the cause of the rise from 1.9% to 3.6% rather than merely screening the output, and it avoids the delivery delays caused by rework. Pure inspection is rejected as reactive and expensive in time, while prevention has no stated total-cost barrier beyond the $950 per-employee course. A practical sequence is to introduce prevention training first and keep a final inspection before release, so the 1,400 builds are checked without relying on rework. Progress should be judged against the given 3.6% defect rate, the 1.9% prior rate and the 6.5-day delivery time. Because the insert does not state how many of the 35 staff need the $950 course, no total cost is asserted; the decision rests on preventing faults rather than sorting them out later.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of quality control and quality assurance with limited application to KDS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both approaches in the context of KDS.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both approaches with a well-justified decision covering defect rate, rework, cost and delivery time.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how KDS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $280,000 ÷ ($40 − $12) = $280,000 ÷ $28 = 10,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 10,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $40 − $12 = $28. Answer: contribution per unit is $28.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways KDS's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 10,000-unit break-even output with 25,000 units produced, giving a margin of safety of 15,000 units, so managers can judge how much falling demand from small-business clients the studio can absorb before a loss.
2. Use the $28 contribution per unit to test a discount: a 5% cut to $38 leaves $26 contribution, so about 10,769 units (280,000 ÷ 26) would then be needed to cover the $280,000 fixed costs.
3. Average total cost is about $23.2 a unit ($280,000 ÷ 25,000 = $11.2 plus $12), well below the $40 price, leaving room for the $950 per-employee training cost.
4. Labour productivity is about 714 units per worker (25,000 ÷ 35), a baseline for checking whether the $640,000 automated suite really raises output per developer.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 10,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $28 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 15,000 units; discount to $38 leaving $26 contribution and about 10,769 units needed; average total cost of $23.2 against $40; labour productivity of about 714 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KDS's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin and the profit margin for 2024 and 2025. Has KDS's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 45.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 50.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 20.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 25.0%
ROCE 2024 = 16.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 revenue 800, cost of sales 440, gross profit 360; operating profit 160; capital employed 1,000. 2025 revenue 960, cost of sales 480, gross profit 480; operating profit 240; capital employed 1,200. Gross profit ÷ revenue: 360 ÷ 800 and 480 ÷ 960. Operating profit ÷ revenue: 160 ÷ 800 and 240 ÷ 960. Operating profit ÷ capital employed: 160 ÷ 1,000 and 240 ÷ 1,200.

Evaluation: Every indicator is better in 2025. The share of revenue left after direct costs rose from 45.0% to 50.0% because cost of sales increased by only 40 while revenue grew by 160, so the studio is delivering more value per app build. The share retained as operating profit also rose, and the return on the 1,200 of capital employed improved as the $640,000 testing suite began to contribute. This is important given the 3.6% defect rate and 47 monthly complaints, which could otherwise have raised rework costs.

Conclusion: KDS's financial position has improved. Both margins and the return on capital are higher, and the improvement is driven by revenue growing much faster than cost of sales rather than by cutting essential quality spending. Management should now use the stronger margins to fund prevention training and protect the 25,000-unit output target. Management should also monitor interest payable as capital employed grows, to ensure the improvement is not merely the result of cheaper borrowing.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the two margins for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of revenue, cost, profit and capital trends, and a justified conclusion on whether KDS improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KDS of introducing e-commerce payment integration for its app clients.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 250 small-business clients found 44% would pay $2 more per month for priority support and 68% want faster updates, so adding e-commerce payment integration can turn that demand into extra revenue and automate billing for the 1,400 app builds. The additional contribution supports the $280,000 fixed costs and helps justify the $640,000 suite without relying solely on the $40 selling price.

Disadvantage: Building payment integration requires development time when delivery already averages 6.5 days and complaints have reached 47 per month, so it could worsen lateness and distract from fixing the 3.6% defect rate. It may also raise the $12 variable cost per unit through transaction fees, squeezing the $28 contribution, and any payment error would damage trust with small-business clients. The payment feature should be tested against the current 3.6% defect rate before launch, because a faulty checkout would add to the 47 complaints and undermine the $2 premium that 44% of clients accept.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to KDS's survey, delivery time and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.2%, the 6.1% minimum wage increase to $15.70 and the 9.8% rise in cloud-server and software licence costs will affect KDS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.5% to 4.2%): If the $400,000 seven-year bank loan is variable-rate, the additional annual interest is 0.7% × $400,000 = $2,800 a year, shown as 0.007 × $400,000. That is modest next to $280,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed the direct interest effect is nil. The wider risk is dearer future borrowing while KDS still needs to complete the $640,000 suite.

Minimum wage increase (6.1% to $15.70 an hour): The insert gives no hours worked or current pay, so an annual wage bill cannot be invented. The derived measure is productivity: 25,000 units ÷ 35 workers = about 714 units per worker. If developers maintain that output the wage rise can be absorbed; if the 3.6% defect rate forces rework, unit labour costs rise and the $28 contribution falls. The direction is clear but the size cannot be quantified from the data.

Input-cost inflation (9.8% on cloud servers and licences): The insert does not split the $12 variable cost, so an explicit upper bound is 9.8% × $12 = $1.176, about $1.18 per unit. Across 25,000 units that is 25,000 × $1.18 = $29,500 a year. Even a partial pass-through reduces contribution from $28 toward about $26.82, raising the volume needed to cover $280,000 of fixed costs.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in cloud-server and licence costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to all 25,000 units and directly erodes the $28 contribution needed to service the $400,000 loan; the interest rise is only $2,800 a year and the wage effect is unquantifiable and partly offset by productivity. KDS should offset the input rise through the $2 priority-support premium shown in its research.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to KDS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on KDS's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with shown derivations from insert figures and a well-justified greatest-impact judgement.
